name: Jade Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do content and social for a skincare start-up, about thirty people, in an old warehouse with too many plants. In the morning I draft captions and short videos for serums and sunscreen, mostly with AI, then I fix them so they don't sound like a robot wrote them. Afternoons are planning the next launch and arguing with our chemist about what we're legally allowed to say.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love trying new tools, I'm usually the first one to test anything. What's hard is that I'm still not very good at the strategy part, my boss Mira rewrites my campaign plans a lot. I'm quick, but quick isn't the same as good, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that would be a bit disappointing for me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something like, fine, so the tools are useful but not magic, and that's okay. At work I'd keep showing people shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I use AI every single day to draft serum captions, so a plateau just means my favourite tool stays a tool. My job's safe, I've got about a year of savings, and there are loads of start-ups around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and focus on getting better at strategy, since that's what Mira keeps fixing. I'd take a short evening course in brand planning, maybe four hundred for the term. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure you'd still feel in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start-ups fold. If our next round of funding doesn't come through, the whole team could go, AI or not. But I could find another job in a month, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time the tools save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go to the lab more. I want to understand the chemistry, because the best captions come from knowing what the cream actually does.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful, not magic**, and that's fine.
I'd keep showing colleagues **shortcuts** at work.
think: I think a plateau keeps AI as **my favourite tool**, nothing more.
I'd feel **secure** with a year of savings and plenty of start-ups nearby.
do: Take an evening **brand planning** course for about four hundred.
Spend saved time in the **lab** learning what the products do.
feel: **Calm** and slightly bored by how little changes.
S0.quote: I use AI every single day to draft serum captions, so a plateau just means my favourite tool stays a tool.
fieldNote: She's **disappointed**, not relieved, which sets her apart from most juniors.
Her only real risk is the **start-up funding**, and she feels she'd land fast.
She knows she's **quick but not good** at strategy yet.

steps.text: Take a four-hundred evening course in brand planning
Keep drafting captions with AI and spend saved time in the lab

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I actually expect, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting, but the gains have to be shared, or it's just bosses getting richer. I'd post threads about tools and about workers' rights in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm the junior who already does the work of three people with AI, which makes me either very safe or the reason the other two aren't hired. I don't love being that reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who sets up the AI workflow for the whole marketing team. I'd start freelancing on weekends for small brands that can't afford an agency, maybe two clients at three hundred a month each. And I'd join a union for tech and creative workers, even at a start-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited for me, uncomfortable about what it does to people like my friend Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tomas. Who's he to you, and why worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas is my best friend from university, and he's a copywriter at an agency who won't touch AI. He's a better writer than me, honestly, and I can see him being let go while I'm kept. That feels wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join a union at a start-up. Would that go down well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not with the founders. But I'd do it anyway, quietly. If I'm going to be the one who makes three jobs into one, I want someone protecting the other two.

say: I'd call it **exciting**, but insist the **gains are shared**.
I'd post about **tools and workers' rights** in the same week.
think: I think I'm **safe**, because I already do three people's work with AI.
I'd feel guilty being the **reason** others aren't hired.
do: Set up the **AI workflow** for the whole marketing team.
Freelance for **two small brands** at weekends and join a tech workers' **union**.
feel: **Uneasy**: excited for myself, uncomfortable about friends being let go.
S1.quote: I'm the junior who already does the work of three people with AI, which makes me either very safe or the reason the other two aren't hired.
fieldNote: She expects to **keep her job**, so her unease is about others, not herself.
Her **guilt** over replacing colleagues pushes her toward a union.
She's already planning **side income** from small brands.

steps.text: Build the AI content workflow for the whole marketing team
Take two small freelance clients at three hundred a month each
Join a union for tech and creative workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one is actually scary, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a basic income now, not in five years. Online I'd be the person posting how-tos and protest dates side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good at AI tools for two years is like being the best typist the year computers learned to type themselves. My whole job is thinking work on a screen, so it goes at the start, not three years later with the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pile everything into freelancing for small shops while they still need a human to steer the AI, and cut my spending to about half. I'd stop the evening course, it'd be pointless. And I'd volunteer for whatever campaign was pushing for basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but strangely awake. I'd be scared and busy at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, to halve your spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own flat, actually. I'd move in with Asha, my flatmate from before, and split rent. That's six hundred a month gone straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a year saved. Does that make you feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year sounds like a lot until you picture everyone like me looking for work at once. It buys time, not safety.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** now, not in five years.
I'd post **how-tos and protest dates** side by side.
think: I think AI skill becomes **worthless** fast when AI does the whole job.
I'd see my **screen-only work** going first, not three years later.
do: Freelance for **small shops** and cut my spending to about **half**.
Volunteer for a **basic income** campaign and drop the evening course.
feel: **Anxious** but awake, scared and busy at once.
S2.quote: Being good at AI tools for two years is like being the best typist the year computers learned to type themselves.
fieldNote: Her AI skill **stops protecting her** here, and she sees it immediately.
Savings give her **some control**, which keeps her at anxious, not alarmed.
She reaches for **politics** and freelancing at the same moment.

steps.text: Freelance for small shops that still need someone steering AI
Move back in with a flatmate to save six hundred a month
Volunteer for a basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd want to use every month of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the clock is visible now, so governments and companies have no excuse. I'd push the start-up to tell staff what their plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with five years I'd spend my savings on building something I own, not on hoping a skincare brand keeps a junior around. Owning a bit of the thing that uses the AI feels safer than being paid to do the work it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd set up a small content co-op with Tomas and two others, all using AI, owned by us. I'd put about eight thousand of my savings in. I'd keep my job part-time for the first year so I still had a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lot of hope mixed in. I'd probably overwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomas really join, given he won't use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe as the person who checks everything sounds human. He'd hate the tools, but he'd like owning a quarter of a company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op doesn't work by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost eight thousand and learned a lot. I'd still have some savings left, and I'd be 32, which isn't old.

say: I'd say the clock is **visible**, so nobody has an excuse.
I'd push the start-up to share its **plan** with staff.
think: I think **owning** something beats hoping to be kept as a junior.
I'd rather own the thing using AI than **do the work** it replaces.
do: Set up a small **content co-op** with my friend and two others.
Invest about **eight thousand** and keep my job **part-time** for a year.
feel: **Anxious** but hopeful, and likely to overwork.
S3.quote: With five years I'd spend my savings on building something I own, not on hoping a skincare brand keeps a junior around.
fieldNote: Her **progressive** view turns into a co-op, not a solo business.
She accepts losing **eight thousand** as a fair price for learning.
Her plan still relies on **thinking work**, which the end point also takes.

steps.text: Put eight thousand of savings into a four-person content co-op
Run the co-op alongside her day job
Drop to part-time at the skincare start-up for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a real runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a safety net for everyone, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd go to every meeting of the basic income group in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough time to fight for a fair deal, and I'd rather spend the decade fighting than hiding. My job would change a lot, but I'd ride it, and I'd have time to save more and learn the strategy side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the start-up and grow into strategy, using AI more each year. I'd run the freelance work on the side and save half of it. And I'd give real time to the basic income campaign, maybe one evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like something I can get ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you feel mostly fine, when the end point is the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think a decade is enough for the politics to catch up. If there's a decent safety net by 2036, losing my job is a change, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the politics doesn't catch up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll have spent ten years saving and building clients. I'd be poorer than I hoped, but not stuck.

say: I'd say a decade is enough to build a **safety net** for everyone.
I'd attend every **basic income** meeting in town.
think: I think I'd rather spend the decade **fighting** than hiding.
I'd expect my job to **change a lot** but give me time to save.
do: Stay at the start-up and grow into **strategy** with more AI each year.
Save **half** my freelance income and give one evening a week to **campaigning**.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine, because there's time to get ready.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to fight for a fair deal, and I'd rather spend the decade fighting than hiding.
fieldNote: Her calm depends on **politics catching up** in time.
She expects her job to **change, not vanish**, within the decade.
Savings plus **freelance clients** are her backup if the safety net fails.

steps.text: Grow into the strategy role using more AI each year
Keep freelance clients on the side
Save half of the freelance income
Give one evening a week to the basic income campaign

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole advantage disappears overnight. What would help is a basic income or something like it, so people don't have to be lucky. Nobody should have to be lucky with savings to survive this, and I know I only feel brave because I've got a year in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who people feel guilty about. I'd be fine in a lot of these pictures, partly because I'm the one replacing people like Tomas. That's going to change friendships, not just jobs.

headlineQuote: Nobody should have to be lucky with savings to survive this, and I know I only feel brave because I've got a year in the bank.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old **content marketer** at a skincare start-up who uses AI daily.
She has about **a year saved** and is quick but still weak at **strategy**.
She stays calm or uneasy in the slower pictures and only turns **anxious** when AGI comes.
She feels **guilty** about replacing friends like Tomas and turns that into union and co-op plans.
She pins her hopes on a **basic income** and her own freelance clients.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her advantage with AI tools vanishes overnight.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or similar, so surviving doesn't depend on **luck**.
